scenes.text: Can mathematics and game strategies explain why nations go to war?
scenes.narration: Can we predict world politics like a science experiment or a game of chess? Let us explore how scholars turned foreign policy into systems and rational strategies.

scenes.text: Studying a cricket tournament requires looking at team dynamics, not just one batsman.
scenes.narration: As an everyday analogy, think of a cricket tournament: you cannot understand the game by watching one batsman alone. You must study pitch conditions, team rivalries, and how every move triggers a countermove.

scenes.name: Morton Kaplan
scenes.idea: Studied international politics as an overarching system using ten distinct models.
scenes.narration: Morton Kaplan wanted a grand, scientific theory of international politics free from ideology. Instead of analyzing separate foreign policies, he mapped out ten models governed by rules, capabilities, and information.

scenes.heading: Two Contrasting Kaplan Models
scenes.narration: Look at how Kaplan contrasted different worlds. In a hierarchical model, one superpower dominates everyone, whereas in a unit veto system, every single nation holds equal power to destroy.

scenes.heading: Chicken Game Dilemma
scenes.narration: Thomas Schelling applied game theory to predict rational behavior during conflicts. In the 1962 Cuban missile crisis, leaders faced a Chicken Game: swerve to prevent catastrophe, or hold on to protect prestige.

scenes.heading: Prisoner's Dilemma Nuclear Choice
scenes.narration: Here is the trick behind the Prisoner's Dilemma. Because of a huge trust deficit, neither India nor Pakistan could risk restraint, so both chose defection and built nuclear weapons to avoid the worst outcome.

scenes.heading: Decision-Making Approach Focus
items: Pioneered by Snyder, Bruck, and Sapin
Treats foreign policy as decision-making process
Proactive search for problems and alternatives
Shaped by environmental and organisational factors
scenes.narration: Finally, Richard Snyder and his colleagues argued that foreign policy is an active decision-making process. Governments do not merely react to crises; they proactively weigh organisational habits and environmental factors to pick alternatives.

items: Kaplan modeled international politics as an overarching system
Game theory models strategic choices under trust deficits
Decision-making analyzes internal and external policy factors
scenes.narration: Remember these three big ideas: Kaplan viewed international relations as systems, game theory explains rational strategies under distrust, and decision-making unpacks how leaders choose alternatives.
